subject: The Papyrus · Egypt's stock market is 143 years old — and a lesson in reading numbers
html:
Older than you'd guess, and a trap for the unwary

Egypt has had a stock exchange since 1883, when the Alexandria bourse opened; Cairo followed in 1903. By the 1940s the combined Egyptian exchange ranked, by some accounts, the fifth most active in the world. Then the socialist nationalisations of the 1950s emptied it, and it sat essentially dormant from 1961 to 1992 — three lost decades — before reopening. (Sources: Egypt State Information Service; African Markets.)

The number that looks like a miracle

The headline index, the EGX30, closed 2020 at about 10,845 points. Five years later, at the end of 2025, it closed near 41,829 — almost quadruple. On paper, one of the great bull runs anywhere. (Source: EGX 30 annual data via Wikipedia; afrivestia.)

Now read it properly

Here's the lesson every data person eventually learns: a number means nothing without its unit. That index is measured in Egyptian pounds — and over those same years the pound lost roughly two-thirds of its dollar value (from about 15.7 to the dollar to around 50). Much of the “quadrupling” isn't companies growing four-fold; it's the currency shrinking, with money flowing into shares as a shelter from inflation. Measured in dollars, the same market is roughly flat. The EGX30 even jumped most sharply in 2023 — the year of the steepest devaluation. (Sources: EGX 30 index; Central Bank of Egypt / market rates. This is history and education, not investment advice.)

Nominal versus real; local currency versus hard currency. It's the difference between a chart that impresses you and one you actually understand — and it's exactly the kind of thing you learn by querying the numbers yourself.

A 143-year-old market, and a reminder to always ask “in what units?” See you next month.
